title: Guessing and explaining meaning
subtitle: context clues, false friends, It's a kind of ...
summary: Learn to work out the meaning of an unfamiliar word from its context, its parts and other languages you know, and to explain a word you cannot name.

lesson.heading: Clues in the context
lesson.text: You do not need to look up every new word. Your **background knowledge** of the situation and the **words around** the unfamiliar word usually tell you enough.

examples.text: If you already know there has just been an **earthquake** in a big city, you will understand the word the first time you hear it on the news.
Tara picked one tall yellow **gladiolus** to put in her new vase.
examples.note: You have never seen the word, but the context makes it clear it is a flower.

examples.text: Kate carried in a delicious chicken soup in a large **tureen** and we enjoyed several bowls each.
examples.note: a tureen must be a kind of very large bowl used for soup

lesson.heading: Grammatical clues
lesson.text: The position of the word in the sentence tells you its **word class**, and that already narrows the meaning down a great deal.

examples.text: Alejandro is very **superstitious** and would never walk under a ladder.
examples.note: It comes after is and very, so it must be an adjective.

examples.text: Mike came **gingerly** down the stairs, trying to avoid all the broken glass.
examples.note: It describes how he came, so it must be an adverb: carefully and cautiously.

examples.text: We would **clamber** over the farmer's gate and go right to the edge.

lesson.heading: Clues in the word itself
lesson.text: A great many English words are built from other words you already know. Split a long word into its parts and the meaning often falls out.

examples.text: a **headscarf** = a scarf worn on the head
a **cement-mixer** = the machine used for mixing cement
a **tree-lined** street = a street with trees along both sides

lesson.heading: Prefixes and suffixes as clues
rows: to send it to a different address
a report that comes out twice a month, or every two months
the person who used to be my boss
feelings that are hostile to tourists
letters that have not been delivered

lesson.heading: Other languages and false friends
lesson.text: If your first language is of Latin or Germanic origin, many English words will resemble words you already know - and English has borrowed from many other languages too. But beware of **false friends**: words that look the same but mean something different.

examples.text: **gift** in English means a present, but *Gift* in German means poison.
**longevity** contains *long* and *life*: it means living a long life.
A tortoise has a **lifespan** of more than 150 years.
examples.note: lifespan = the time from birth to death

lesson.heading: Explaining an unknown word
lesson.text: When you cannot name something, describe it. These four patterns will get you out of almost any gap in your vocabulary.

examples.text: **It's probably something (a bit) like** a chair, but with no back.
**It's got to be something you use for** cleaning the kitchen floor.
**It's a kind of** bird / musical instrument / building.

lesson.text: Guess first, check afterwards. If you reach for a dictionary at every unknown word you will never build the skill of reading through one.

exercises.prompt: A tortoise is a shelled reptile famed for its slowness and longevity. Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.right: an animal like a snake or crocodile

exercises.prompt: The Giant Tortoise may attain over 1.5 metres in length. *Attain* here means ___.
exercises.explanation: Attain = reach. The context is a measurement, so nothing else fits.

exercises.prompt: They may have a lifespan of more than 150 years. A *lifespan* is the time from birth to ___.
exercises.explanation: Life + span: the length of time something lives.

exercises.prompt: Above the trees a buzzard hangs for a moment on the wind before soaring towards the hills. What is a buzzard?
options: It must be a kind of bird.
It must be a kind of tool.
It must be a kind of bowl.
It must be a kind of flower.
exercises.explanation: Only a bird hangs on the wind and soars.

exercises.prompt: Using a large chisel and a hammer, Jack knocked down the old garden wall. What is a chisel?
options: A kind of tool used for chipping away at something.
exercises.explanation: It is used together with a hammer, so it has to be a tool.

exercises.prompt: The water vole is one of the most rapidly declining creatures in Britain. What is a vole?
options: A kind of small animal, something like a mouse.
exercises.explanation: The word *creatures* tells you it is an animal.

exercises.prompt: Match each compound with a simpler explanation.

pairs.left: up to my eyes in work

exercises.prompt: Does the prefix put the event before or after the main word?
Letters that have not been delivered are ___ letters.
Anger that cannot be controlled is ___ anger.
exercises.explanation: un- + control + -able: not able to be controlled.

exercises.statement: *Gift* in English and *Gift* in German are false friends.
exercises.explanation: Correct: in English a gift is a present, but in German Gift means poison.

exercises.statement: If you redirect a letter, you open it and read it.
exercises.explanation: To redirect a letter is to send it on to a different address.

exercises.prompt: Explain a word you don't know the name of.
exercises.answer: It's got to be something you use for cleaning the kitchen floor.
exercises.explanation: It's got to be something you use for ... is a useful way of describing an object whose name you don't know.
